questions.question: Which three components make up the complete view of a virtual reality system?
options: The organism, the virtual environment, and the VR hardware
The organism, the VR hardware, and the user's sensory experience
The organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world
The VR hardware, the virtual environment, and the surrounding physical world
questions.explanation: The complete view includes the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.

questions.question: In the complete view of a virtual reality system, what is the data flow from the organism to the VR hardware called?
options: Stimulation
Bidirectional exchange
Environmental monitoring
Tracking
questions.explanation: Data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking.

questions.question: In the complete view of a virtual reality system, what is the data flow from the VR hardware to the organism called?
options: Tracking
Environmental monitoring
Bidirectional exchange
Stimulation
questions.explanation: Data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation.

questions.question: Why is the organism considered equally important as the VR hardware in the complete view of a virtual reality system?
options: Because the user is more important than the hardware
Because the user is unaffected by the surrounding physical world
Because the user is always present
Because the user controls all data flows in the system
questions.explanation: The organism, typically the human user, is equally important to account for and cannot be omitted because the user is always present.

questions.question: Which data flow in a VR system carries hardware-generated stimuli to the user?
options: Surrounding-world output flow
Tracking data flow
Stimulation data flow
Surrounding-world input flow
questions.explanation: In a VR system, the stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli to the user, while tracking data flow carries user motion information to the hardware.

questions.question: What role does the tracking data flow play in a VR system?
options: It supplies computer-generated sensory experiences directly to the user's organs
It blocks real-world sensory inputs from reaching the user's sensory organs
It measures how fully immersed the user feels in the virtual environment
It lets VR hardware adjust its stimuli using tracked user motions
questions.explanation: The tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so that the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.

questions.question: Which tracked user action is described as commonly used and the most important to track in VR?
options: Head tracking
Controller movements
Button presses
Eye movements
questions.explanation: Head tracking is commonly used and is the most important tracking target, although button presses, eye movements, controller movements, and other body movements may also be tracked.

questions.question: Which three components make up the overall virtual reality system?
options: The displays, the sensors, and the computers
The user, the stimulation data, and the tracking data
The HMD, the controller, and the virtual world
The user, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical environment
questions.explanation: The overall VR system is said to have three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.

questions.question: Why is the surrounding physical environment treated as part of a VR system?
options: The hardware must track every object in the room to create immersion
Real-world stimuli can affect user behavior while interacting with the virtual world
Head movements are the main data needed to update the display
The environment supplies the virtual graphics that the HMD displays
questions.explanation: The environment is part of the system because the user may respond to real-world stimuli and may not be completely detached from the real world.

questions.question: How can the user change the surrounding physical environment during VR interaction?
options: By moving virtual objects with a handheld controller
By changing the virtual scene shown in the HMD
By receiving stimulation data from the VR hardware
By moving physically while interacting with the virtual world
questions.explanation: A user's physical movement while interacting with the virtual world may change the surrounding physical environment.

questions.question: When may VR hardware track objects in the surrounding physical environment instead of the user directly?
options: When interaction with those objects is part of the experience
When the user needs to be completely detached from the real world
When the hardware must reduce the effects of light, sound, and smell
When head tracking is unavailable or too expensive
questions.explanation: VR hardware may track objects in the environment instead of the user directly when interaction with those objects is part of the experience.

questions.question: What does a robotic arm used by an immersive VR application show about VR hardware?
options: VR hardware is limited to the computer, HMD, and controller
VR hardware is only an output device that stimulates the user's senses
VR hardware is only an input device that tracks the user's movements
VR hardware can change the surrounding physical environment, and that change may affect the user
questions.explanation: A robotic arm can change the position of objects in the environment, showing that VR hardware may deal with objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than being limited to the computer, HMD, or controller.

questions.question: Which three categories are the major components of VR hardware?
options: Displays, sensors, and computers
Hand input devices, non-hand input devices, and displays
Displays, cameras, and robotic arms
User, hardware, and physical environment
questions.explanation: VR hardware is described as having displays as output devices, sensors as input devices, and computers as processing devices.

questions.question: In VR hardware, what does a display or output device mean in the broad sense?
options: Any device that processes inputs and produces outputs for the user
Any device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs
Only a screen that shows visual content
Any device that tracks the user's movements
questions.explanation: A display/output device is not limited to visual displays; it includes any device that produces sensory output for the user.

questions.question: Why are sensors classified as input devices in VR hardware?
options: They process inputs and produce outputs for the user
They require the user's hands to operate
They produce output that stimulates the user's sensory organs
They track the user's input and extract information from the real world
questions.explanation: A sensor/input device is a tracking device that tracks user input and extracts real-world information, with the discussion restricted to sensors tracking user movements.

questions.question: What is a computer or processing device in VR hardware?
options: A device that processes inputs and produces outputs for the user to perceive the world
A device that tracks the user's movements in the real world
A device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs
A device that changes the surrounding physical environment
questions.explanation: The computer/processing device processes inputs and produces outputs so that the user can perceive the world.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the five broad categories of VR hand input devices?
options: Tracked handheld controllers
Body-movement sensors
Eye-tracking devices
Head-mounted displays
questions.explanation: VR hand input devices are divided into world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.

questions.question: What capability of tracked handheld controllers helps avoid the break-in presence that can occur with non-tracked handheld controllers?
options: They require the user to keep hands in front of an IR camera
They provide only discrete button and trigger input
Six-degree-of-freedom tracking of their movement in 3D space
They are worn on the fingers instead of held in the hand
questions.explanation: Non-tracked handheld controllers are not tracked in 3D space, so virtual hands may not move with the user. Tracked handheld controllers have 6DoF tracking, so their movement can be reflected in the virtual world.

questions.question: Why may tracked handheld controllers not let users fully touch and feel passive virtual objects?
options: The controller is not tracked in three-dimensional space
The user does not hold any device in the hand
The user must keep the hands in front of a camera
The user’s hands are occupied with the controller
questions.explanation: Because the hands are occupied with the controller, users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction.

questions.question: What problem is specifically tied to recognizing many gestures with hand-worn input devices?
options: The fingers are restricted to fingertip-only sensors
The device must be attached to a low-cost HMD to work
Users may need to recalibrate often or learn and remember many gestures
The user’s hands must remain visible to a wide-angle camera
questions.explanation: When many gestures are possible, hand-worn devices may require frequent recalibration or force users to remember many gestures, which can be difficult for some users.

questions.question: What enables bare-hand input to leave the user’s hands completely free?
options: A tracked controller reports six degrees of freedom
A data glove processes continuous bend-sensor data
An HMD uses head yaw, roll, and pitch to infer hand gestures
Computer vision detects the hand gestures and converts them into commands
questions.explanation: In bare-hand input, the system tracks the user’s bare hand with computer vision and translates detected gestures into virtual-environment commands, so no wearable or controller is needed.

items.title: Order the signal steps of a Leap Motion hand-tracking sensor
steps: Infrared light reflects from the user's hands

Software converts the signals into gestures

questions.question: What does non-hand-based input mean for VR input devices?
options: Input from hand-worn devices only
Input from hand-held controllers only
Input from tracked hand gestures only
Input from body parts other than the hand
questions.explanation: Non-hand-based input devices capture input from parts of the body other than the hand, including head movement, eye gaze, voice, and body movement.

questions.question: How does an HMD that doubles as a head-tracking device infer input to change the view?
options: It uses sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch
It uses sensors that detect hand pinch gestures
It uses sensors that record the user's voice
It uses sensors that track where the user is looking
questions.explanation: A head-mounted display can double as a head tracking device when its sensors detect yaw, roll, and pitch to infer input that changes the view.

questions.question: What information do eye tracking devices help a system understand?
options: The exact position of a tracked handheld controller
The user's head yaw, roll, and pitch
The user's hand posture and gestures
Where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving
questions.explanation: Eye tracking devices track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, so the system can infer what action to take.

questions.question: What is the Midas touch problem in eye-tracking-based input?
options: The system cannot distinguish an intentional hand gesture from a habitual hand rest
The system cannot distinguish an intentional head turn from a habitual head rest
The system cannot distinguish an intentional controller press from a habitual grip
The system cannot distinguish an intentional selection gaze from a habitual blank gaze
questions.explanation: The Midas touch problem is the inability to differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze, which can cause unintended selections or actions.

questions.question: Why is multimodal input generally preferable to eye-tracking-only input?
options: It removes eye tracking from the interaction entirely
It makes head tracking the only way to change the view
It adds other input forms to avoid unintentional gaze-based selections
It prevents users from using hand-based input
questions.explanation: Multimodal input uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking, which is preferable because eye tracking alone can select objects or perform actions from unintentional gazes.

questions.question: What is the reason for understanding VR hardware from an overall system point of view?
options: To ensure that the user's senses are blocked from the real-world environment.
To make untracked handheld controllers produce corresponding virtual hand movements.
To identify the requirements and the hardware to look for based on how system components interact.
To classify VR systems as non-immersive, semi-immersive, or fully immersive.
questions.explanation: VR hardware should be considered with the multiple system components and their interactions so that the needed requirements and suitable hardware can be known.

questions.question: What are the three major hardware components of any virtual reality system?
options: Input, output, and processor.
Non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive.
Artificial environment, sensory experience, and user action.
Head movement, eye gaze, and voice.
questions.explanation: The major hardware components of any VR system are input, output, and processor.

questions.question: Why does a complete view of a virtual reality system include the surrounding physical environment in addition to the user and the virtual reality hardware?
questions.reference_answer: The complete view of a VR system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world. The environment is included because the user may respond to real-world stimuli and is not completely detached, so it can affect the user's behavior. The user's physical movement can change the environment, and VR hardware can also change it, for example by moving objects with a robotic arm.

questions.question: How does the tracking data flow help a virtual reality system satisfy the requirement that a user's actions partially determine what happens in the environment?
questions.reference_answer: A virtual reality system is defined by an artificial environment in which the user's actions partially determine what happens. The tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motion, so the hardware can adjust the stimulation data flow carrying stimuli to the user. Head tracking is commonly used and is the most important tracked motion, while tracking may also include button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

questions.question: Why can a tracked handheld controller reduce break-in presence while still limiting the user's tangible interaction with passive virtual objects?
questions.reference_answer: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. A non-tracked handheld controller is not tracked in three-dimensional space, so the user's untracked hand movements may not produce a corresponding change in the virtual hands, causing break-in presence and affecting presence. A tracked handheld controller has six degrees of freedom tracking, so break-in presence is avoided, but the user's hands are occupied with the controller and cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

questions.question: What makes bare-hand input more natural than controller-based hand input, and what practical problems can a Leap Motion device introduce?
questions.reference_answer: Bare-hand input is the most natural hand input because computer vision tracks the user's bare hand, detects gestures, and leaves the hands free without any worn device. The Leap Motion device is an infrared hand-tracking sensor with light-emitting diodes and wide-angle cameras, and it can be attached to a head-mounted display to support low-cost head-mounted displays. However, it can cause fatigue if the hands are held in front of its sensor, requires the hand to be in the line of sight of its camera, and may have inconsistent gesture recognition across users.
